vocab.articleQuote: Its educational establishment espoused “play-based” learning, especially for younger children.
vocab.meaning: To **espouse** an idea, cause, or way of doing things is to adopt it as your own and support it openly — the word shares a root with *spouse*, as if you had married the idea. Finland's education leaders espoused play-based learning: they didn't just permit it, they embraced it and promoted it as their official philosophy. You espouse things you actively stand behind, not things you merely tolerate.
examples: Our coach espouses the idea that defense wins championships, so every practice starts with defensive drills.
After the debate unit, half the class began to espouse positions just to argue, whether they believed them or not.

vocab.articleQuote: Finland’s critics posit that the high marks it achieved in 2000 in fact reflected old-fashioned educational approaches that were still prevalent in its schools well into the 1990s
vocab.meaning: To **posit** something is to put it forward as a claim or explanation — offered seriously, as a basis for argument, but not yet proven. Finland's critics posit an explanation for its 2000 triumph: the old teaching methods, not the new ones, deserved the credit. It is the workhorse verb of research and journalism — scientists, historians, and columnists posit theories all the time, and the word quietly signals *this is a proposal, judge it yourself*.
examples: Scientists posit that a ninth planet exists far beyond Neptune, based on the strange orbits of distant objects.
My sister posits that the cafeteria serves its best food on days when parents visit — she has been collecting evidence all semester.

vocab.articleQuote: Covid or screens do not explain the disparity, given that these scourges have affected all children in Britain in a fairly similar way.
vocab.meaning: A **scourge** is something that causes widespread suffering or damage — the word originally meant a whip, and it still carries that sting. Writers reach for it when a problem lashes a whole population: the scourge of war, of malaria, of misinformation. The article uses it for covid and smartphones — two afflictions that have battered every child's schooling, which is exactly why they can't explain why Scotland fell while England held up.
examples: Mosquitoes are the scourge of every summer camping trip, no matter how much repellent we pack.
Cheating apps became such a scourge that the school finally banned phones during exams.

concepts.name: PISA
concepts.articleQuote: The OECD’s project, known as PISA, takes a measure of young people’s aptitudes as they approach the end of their compulsory school days.
concepts.meaning:
How would you know whether a whole country's schools are getting better or worse? You can't compare grades — an A in Texas, a 9 in Finland, and an A* in England measure different things on different tests. So the OECD, a club of 38 mostly rich countries that collects statistics so its members can compare themselves, built a common yardstick: **PISA**, the Programme for International Student Assessment. Every three years, a large sample of 15-year-olds — the same age everywhere, near the end of compulsory schooling — sits the same tests in reading, mathematics, and science. Because everyone takes the same test at the same age, the scores can be lined up into a league table of school systems: this round, four rich provinces of China came top, with Singapore, Macau, Taiwan, and Japan close behind, and Estonia the best performer in the West.

The scale needs one decoder: about **20 points equals roughly one full year of learning**. That converts abstract scores into something you can feel — when the article says 15-year-olds in rich countries now test where 14-year-olds did a decade ago, it means the average teenager has lost about a year of ability. So when a headline mentions PISA scores rising or falling, you now know exactly what's being claimed: same test, same age, dozens of countries — the closest thing the world has to a report card for entire school systems.

concepts.name: Progressive education
concepts.articleQuote: It argued that teachers should spend less time talking in front of blackboards and more time helping pupils work things out for themselves.
concepts.meaning:
In 2000 Finland shocked everyone by topping the first PISA table, and education ministers flew to Helsinki to learn its secret. What Finland preached was **progressive education**: a century-old movement holding that children learn best by discovering things for themselves — through play, projects, and open-ended exploration — rather than by sitting in rows while a teacher explains facts at the blackboard and tests them on it. The rival tradition, often called *knowledge-rich* schooling or *direct instruction*, argues the reverse: you can't think critically about things you don't know, so children need facts taught explicitly, packed into memory, and checked with rigorous exams.

The article delivers a twist on both. Since 2000, almost no country's scores have fallen as steeply as Finland's — its critics posit that the famous results actually came from old-fashioned teaching still lingering in its classrooms, not the progressive ideas it advertised. Meanwhile England did the opposite of the fashion: it made curriculums more fact-filled, toughened exams and inspections, and steered teachers back toward tested methods — and its teenagers now rank in the world's top ten in all three subjects. The takeaway travels well beyond this article: nearly every fight about schools — homework, testing, phonics, group projects — is this same century-old argument between discovery and direct teaching, wearing different clothes.

quiz.question: What did the latest round of PISA results show for rich countries?
options: Scores rebounded now that the pandemic is well in the past
Scores fell further, with the decline in literacy actually speeding up
Scores held steady everywhere except East Asia
Scores fell only in countries that kept schools closed longest
quiz.explanation: Policymakers hoped for a rebound, but scores in rich countries fell further — and in literacy the decline is accelerating.

quiz.question: On the PISA scale, about how much is 20 points worth?
options: One month of learning
One semester of learning
One full year of learning
Four years of learning
quiz.explanation: The rule of thumb is that 20 points is roughly what an average pupil gains in a full year of learning — the decoder that makes PISA scores meaningful.

quiz.question: Finland's educational establishment 'espoused' play-based learning. What does espoused mean?
options: Quietly abandoned
Adopted and openly supported
Carefully tested in experiments
Reluctantly tolerated
quiz.explanation: To espouse an idea is to adopt it as your own and champion it — Finland made play-based learning its official philosophy.

quiz.question: Why is the comparison between Scotland and England so revealing?
options: Scotland spends far less per pupil than England does
Scottish pupils sit completely different tests from English ones
Covid and screens hit both similarly, so the different results point at their different school policies
England's schools have much smaller classes than Scotland's
quiz.explanation: Since covid and screens affected all of Britain's children in a fairly similar way, Scotland falling behind while England held up points at their starkly different policies — Scotland actually spends more per pupil.

quiz.question: According to the article, what do East Asian school systems generally do differently from Western ones?
options: They keep classes as small as possible by hiring many teachers
They choose to have fewer teachers, whom they pay more and train more intensely
They rely more heavily on educational software in classrooms
They test their pupils far less often
quiz.explanation: Asian countries are much less obsessed with small classes: fewer, better-paid, better-trained teachers — the opposite of America's add-more-staff approach.
